paragraphs.source_en: The place was surrounded on every side by rivers. To the north, the Kamo, Shira, Katsura, Yodo, and Uji rivers converged here to form one great waterway, while the Domyoji and Yamato rivers flowed ceaselessly into it from the southeast. Boats large and small, of every shape and kind, plied the river; even vessels from Ming China, the West, and Korea came and went.

units.source_en: The place was surrounded on every side by rivers.

paragraphs.source_en: At the heart of the Mido stood a square compound belonging to the temple, some eight cho across. The compound was itself the equal of a castle, and the natural rivers around it served as moats; it was truly a strategic stronghold.

paragraphs.source_en: Pilgrims arrived in an unbroken stream, each chanting the Buddha’s name. The present master of the Mido was Shonyo, Rennyo’s grandson. Dwelling within this fortified Mido, he could issue commands from here as though ruling a state within the state.

paragraphs.source_en: At that moment, a man who looked like a samurai stood in the shade of the cloister. He wore a traveling hat against the blazing sun, and beneath its brim his eyes continually studied the worshippers. His dust-covered clothes had long since lost their color, and the lacquer had peeled from his scabbard. He must have come a great distance, for his straw sandals were worn to tatters.

paragraphs.source_en: His shoulders were broad, but his waist was remarkably slender. Holding the brim of his hat with one hand, he walked from one corner of the Mido to another and surveyed the grounds; then he stopped and stared unblinking at the arriving worshippers.

paragraphs.source_en: As Nobuchika traveled toward Izumo, a strange fancy took hold of him. He began to feel close to Okuni, who had been abandoned by his elder brother and had once mistaken him for Nobumoto. Her bond with his brother had been brief, while she and Nobuchika seemed destined to endure hardship together.

paragraphs.source_en: The journey from the capital to Izumo took two months. During that time his loneliness deepened until not for a moment could he forget Okuni’s voice and breath, or even the scent of her body.

paragraphs.source_en: Nobuchika strolled beyond the cloister. The pilgrims came without end. Each face bore its own sorrow and suffering. At the sight, Okuni’s face rose once more before Nobuchika’s eyes.

paragraphs.source_en: Early the next morning, Nobuchika fled Izumo as though escaping for his life. Only later did he learn that this world held troubles far greater than those of the daimyo. He began to understand the lives of ordinary people: utterly ignorant of what tomorrow might bring, they lived like insects and were slaughtered like insects, passing every day in a waking nightmare.

paragraphs.source_en: The holy Rennyo had built this Ishiyama Mido because he was resolved to save the common people. Now his grandson, the holy Shonyo, presided as abbot and issued commands from here to believers throughout the country—but did he truly possess the power to save all the people? His mind crowded with doubts, Nobuchika was about to leave the turret when another voice called him back.

paragraphs.source_en: Cities usually grew as political power strengthened, but this place was entirely different. From the very beginning it had opposed political authority, displaying signs of defiance everywhere. The streets and markets of Osaka gradually spread outward around the Mido, extending ever farther. paragraphs.source_en: Nobuchika sat to Otoshi’s right and watched the two men’s every movement. The composed and handsome Hataro contrasted so sharply with this eccentric, who looked as though he had just crawled from a muddy farm ditch, that Nobuchika found it amusing. Yet he could not have said exactly what was so funny. Both brimmed with vitality, yet appeared extraordinarily calm. They were as incompatible as fire and water, yet from deep within them both emanated a strange serenity.
